title: Roman Numeral Workshop
description: Build numerals from lettered tiles, and find out which combinations the rules simply refuse.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

writeup.why: Write numbers the way a clock face does, using seven letters and three rules.
writeup.look: A tray of lettered tiles with their values underneath, and a rail above where the numeral is built.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Roman Numeral Workshop' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: what the rail is worth so far, in ink, rewritten every time a tile lands or leaves, with the number of tiles on the rail counted beside it; it is the one place the total is written, and it never reads as a score. On the third and fourth phases a second line under it counts the refusals and names the rule of the last one. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The build rail is 860 by 150 at 64,232, a ruled rail on the paper colour with a stop drawn at its left hand end; a tile that lands takes its place on the rail at 84 by 108 at a pitch of 92, so nine tiles fit along it and the longest numeral this chapter asks for fits exactly. The ledger is 226 by 150 at 924,232: one line per tile in the order they landed, the letter and the amount it brings, with a bar drawn at the left of each line, and a line that takes away carries its bar drawn back to front, so adding and subtracting are told apart by shape before any colour; a subtractive pair on the rail is ringed amber, because that pair is what settles the reading. The refusal strip is 860 by 64 at 64,398 and stands empty until a tile is refused, when it prints the rule that refused it in words with the refused tile drawn hollow at its left edge; the place on the rail that tile wanted is left as a hollow outline, so what was refused and where it wanted to go are both still on the stage. The reference card is 226 by 330 at 924,398, seven ruled rows, letter at the left and value at the right, in order of value, and it never closes; its back carries the six subtractive pairs and turns over on the fourth phase. The direction switch is 220 by 64 at 64,488, number into numeral at one end and numeral into number at the other, and the target card is 620 by 64 at 304,488, holding whichever of the two the phase has asked for. The tray is 860 by 150 at 64,580 with seven tiles 108 by 108 at a pitch of 120 from x 74, each letter in ink at 72 tall with its value under it; a tile drawn out of the tray leaves its outline behind and the outline refills at once, because the tray never runs out and no letter is ever used up. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across where a numeral has to be read back as a number, on the first, second and third phases; where a number has to be built the numeral is built on the rail itself and the pad carries the seven letter keys instead, in order of value, which drop that tile onto the right hand end of the rail. On the fourth phase the letter keys stay and a strip of the six allowed pairs sits under them, so a pair can be dropped as one press. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the ones period is deep blue, the thousands period green, the lakhs period vermilion and the millions period rose; whatever settles the answer on this stage is amber; a zero that is only holding a place open is grey; and chrome never borrows one of them, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
writeup.finish: The card shows the numerals the child built, and the combinations the rules refused with the reason beside each one.

phases.win: every tile has been matched to its value at least once
phases.does: matches each letter to its value and drops single tiles into the rail
phases.goal: every Roman numeral is built from seven letters and no others
phases.says: Seven letters, and no more. Find the one worth fifty.
phases.check: Without looking at the card, which letter is worth fifty, and which one is worth five hundred?
phases.feels: there is nothing here to work out, only something to know
phases.hands: Copy the seven letters and their values onto a card by hand, in order of value, and leave the card on the table for the rest of the topic; then cover the values with a finger and read the letters off it.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many letters are there altogether? Second rung, the phase's: which of them is nearest in value to the one you want? Third rung: the tray is cut to three tiles with their values showing and the child picks from those. The reference card stays open behind all three, because this is a lookup and not a puzzle.

wrong.why: every other number in the chapter has had a way of being written, so a value as ordinary as this looks as though it must have a letter of its own.
wrong.move: hunts the tray for a letter worth twenty and finds nothing to pick up.
wrong.screen: the seven tiles lift a little together and set themselves down in order of value, and the steps between the values light one after another, one, then five, then ten, then fifty, so the gaps are shown to be part of the system. The rail keeps whatever is already on it.

wrong.why: everything else in this chapter has been worked out from something else, so guessing feels like the right kind of effort to be making.
wrong.move: works out what a letter is worth from the letter before it rather than reading it off the card.
wrong.screen: the reference card draws itself open row by row down the right of the working area, letter and value, and the row for the letter in hand lights and stays lit while the tile is held. Nothing on the rail is touched and nothing is marked.

phases.screen: the tray of seven tiles with the reference card open beside it
phases.soWhat: Seven letters carry fixed values, and every numeral is built from those seven and no others.
phases.concept: Seven letters do all the work

phases.win: the numeral reads correctly and the running total matches
phases.does: drops smaller tiles to the right and watches the total climb
phases.goal: a smaller letter to the right of a bigger one is added
phases.says: Put the smaller one on the right. Watch the total go up.
phases.check: Read this numeral to me, and for each letter say whether you added it or took it away, and why.
phases.feels: the order the tiles sit in turns out to be the whole of the reading
phases.hands: Lay two coins of different value on the table with the bigger one at the left, then add a third coin to the right of them, and say the running total out loud as each one goes down.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which side of the bigger letter is the smaller one standing on? Second rung, the phase's: does that side add or take away? Third rung: the rail is cut to two tiles and the child gives the total for that pair alone. The reference card and the pad stay open.

wrong.why: taking away is the rule that gets the most attention, and smallness looks like the thing it depends on.
wrong.move: takes the smaller letter away wherever it is standing, because it is the smaller one.
wrong.screen: the pair on the rail is ringed amber and the ring is drawn round the smaller tile's place rather than round the tile itself, so it is the side it stands on that lights; the ledger line for that tile is rewritten with its bar the right way round and the total climbs to what it should be. The child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the total comes to the same whichever order the letters are added in, and so it does.
wrong.move: builds the numeral with the small letters first, writing it up from its smallest part.
wrong.screen: the tiles slide along the rail into order of value, the biggest at the left, without one of them leaving the rail; the ledger rewrites itself in the new order with the same total standing at its foot, and the rule prints under the rail that a numeral is written from the biggest letter down.

phases.screen: the rail holding a bigger tile with space to its right
phases.soWhat: A smaller letter to the right of a bigger one is added, and a numeral is written from the biggest letter down.
phases.concept: A smaller letter on the right is added

phases.win: the fourth tile is refused and the rule is named on screen
phases.does: tries to add a fourth of the same letter and reads the refusal
phases.goal: repetition means addition, and three is the limit
phases.says: Try one more of the same. What does the rule card say?
phases.check: Why is forty not written as four of the ten letter, and what is it written as instead?
phases.feels: the arithmetic works perfectly and the numeral is still not allowed
phases.hands: Write four of the same letter in a row on paper and say its value out loud four times over, then look along the rule card together and cross the row out.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many of that letter are already on the rail? Second rung, the phase's: what does the rule card give as the limit? Third rung: the rail is left holding three of the letter and the tray offers only the tiles that could lawfully come next. The rule card stays open and nothing on the rail is taken away.

wrong.why: three of them added up perfectly well, so a fourth ought to add up too, and the arithmetic of it is not wrong.
wrong.move: drops a fourth tile of the same letter onto the rail.
wrong.screen: the tile stops a tile's height above the place it wanted and hangs there while the refusal strip prints the rule, that a letter may be repeated three times at most; the three tiles already down are left exactly as they are, and the fourth lifts back to the tray leaving its outline hollow in the gap.

wrong.why: the rule just met allowed three of a letter, so two of anything looks safely inside it.
wrong.move: drops a second of one of the three letters that are never repeated.
wrong.screen: the refusal strip prints the second rule, that this letter is never repeated at all, and the reference card draws a small bar under each of the three letters it covers; the rail keeps the first tile and the pair the child wanted is drawn hollow beside it.

phases.screen: the rail holding three of one letter with the tray still open
phases.soWhat: Repeating a letter adds it again, three is the limit, and three of the seven may not be repeated at all.
phases.concept: A letter may be repeated three times at most

phases.win: the legal pair builds and the illegal one is refused with its reason
phases.does: builds a legal subtractive pair, then tries an illegal one
phases.goal: only six subtractive pairs exist and the rest are not numerals
phases.says: Now put the smaller one on the left. Which pairs are allowed?
phases.check: Write forty-nine as a numeral. Which two pairs did you use, and why not the one letter in front of the fifty?
phases.feels: a lawful pair and an unlawful one look exactly alike until the rail answers
phases.hands: Write the six allowed pairs on the back of the letter card and nothing else, then try to read a numeral built from a pair that is not on the list and see where the reading stops.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which pairs does the card list for the letter in your hand? Second rung, the phase's: is the pair you built one of them? Third rung: the tray offers only the two tiles that this letter may lawfully stand in front of. The list of pairs stays open and nothing built is cleared.

wrong.why: one taken from fifty is forty-nine, and the arithmetic of that is exactly right.
wrong.move: builds forty-nine by standing the one letter to the left of the fifty letter.
wrong.screen: the tile hangs where it was dropped while the refusal strip prints that the one letter may be taken only from the five letter or the ten letter; the reference card turns over to its list of six pairs and the two that begin with that letter light. The rail keeps what was built and the total does not change.

wrong.why: every pair built so far has added, and the two letters look exactly the same whichever side they stand on.
wrong.move: puts the smaller letter on the left and waits for the total to climb.
wrong.screen: the pair is ringed amber and the ledger line for the left hand tile is rewritten with its bar turned back to front; the total drops by that tile's value and the two figures, what it was and what it is now, are printed one under the other beside the ring.

phases.screen: the rail with a smaller tile hovering to the left of a bigger one
phases.soWhat: A smaller letter to the left is subtracted, and only six pairs are allowed: the one letter from the five or the ten, the ten from the fifty or the hundred, and the hundred from the five hundred or the thousand.
phases.concept: A smaller letter on the left is subtracted

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment a fourth tile of the same letter is dropped. It comes down to the rail, reaches the place it wants and stops dead a tile's height above it, and hangs there. The three tiles already down slide apart to open exactly the gap it was aiming for, the rule prints itself under the rail one word at a time, and then the gap closes, the hanging tile lifts back to the tray, and the numeral on the rail is precisely what it was before. Nothing else moves and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. The tray of seven lettered tiles stands along the foot of the working area with each letter's value printed under it, the build rail waits above with its left hand stop drawn, the ledger beside the rail is ruled and empty, and the reference card of the seven letters is open down the right of the working area on every phase, because nothing here is worked out and it is all looked up. On the first phase the rail is empty; on the second one bigger tile already sits at the left of it with clear rail to its right; on the third three of one letter sit on it side by side; on the fourth one bigger tile sits with clear rail to its left. The running count at the top left reads nothing yet, and the slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the tile in the tray that this phase is about gives one small lift while the voice asks for a tile to be lifted and read. That lift is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any tiles, either direction, with every refusal explained rather than blocked in silence. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, converting both ways and testing where the rules stop.
voiceLines: Seven letters in the tray. Lift one and read what it is worth.
Seven letters, and no more. Find the one worth fifty.
Put the smaller one on the right. Watch the total go up.
Try one more of the same. What does the rule card say?
Now put the smaller one on the left. Which pairs are allowed?
The same seven letters. A different rule.
Free play. Any tiles, either way round, and every refusal explained.
Read the rule card again, and then look at what is already on the rail.
You built numerals, and you found what the rules will not let you build.

observations.why: There are seven letters and no others, and not one of them is worked out from another.
observations.soWhat: This is a system to look up, not a system to reason out.
observations.observe: Every numeral built on the rail came out of the same seven tiles.

observations.why: Position decides whether a letter is added or taken away, and size only decides which letter is the smaller one.
observations.soWhat: One question settles every letter: is the smaller one on the left or on the right?
observations.observe: The total climbed when the smaller tile sat to the right and dropped when it sat to the left.

observations.why: Three rules allow a handful of arrangements and shut out everything else.
observations.soWhat: Knowing this system is mostly knowing what is not a numeral at all.
observations.observe: The rail refused far more tiles than it took.

observations.why: The refused tile never landed, so what had already been built was still correct.
observations.soWhat: A refusal is about the one tile in my hand, not about the work I have done.
observations.observe: Not one refusal ever cleared the rail.

phases.screen: the tray of seven tiles with the reference card open beside it
phases.win: every tile has been matched to its value at least once
phases.traceback: The card redraws row by row and the asked rows light with their values; the asked tile lands on the rail, or the right letters are named under the bays.
ladder: Find V on the card. What is written beside it?
Read the card from the top. Which rows say fifty and five hundred?
Find C and M on the card.
Which letter is nearest in value to the one you want?
Run your finger down the card, one row at a time.

phases.screen: the rail holding a bigger tile with space to its right
phases.win: the numeral reads correctly and the running total matches
phases.traceback: Each rail tile writes its amount with an adding bar, then the total climbs to the answer; a build splits by place and the right numeral is laid under the rail.
ladder: Build the tens first, then the ones.
Which side of the bigger letter is the smaller one standing on?
Is any small letter standing on the left of a bigger one?
Does that side add or take away?
Read the rail from the left, one tile at a time.

phases.screen: the rail holding three of one letter with the tray still open
phases.win: the fourth tile is refused and the rule is named on screen
phases.traceback: Each rail tile writes its amount, then the total climbs place by place to the answer; the letters never repeated rise in the tray, take their bars on the card and the strip names them; a build splits by place and the right numeral is laid under the rail.
ladder: How many of each letter are on the rail?
Try two of each letter on the rail. Which ones does it refuse?
Work out the balance first. Then build it place by place, three of a letter at most.
What does the rule card give as the limit?
Take the rail one letter at a time, from the left.

phases.screen: the rail with a smaller tile hovering to the left of a bigger one
phases.win: the legal pair builds and the illegal one is refused with its reason
phases.traceback: Each rail tile writes its amount, a taking-away tile with its bar back to front and its pair ringed amber, then the total climbs to the answer; a build lays the right numeral under the rail, its pair ringed amber and the taking-away tile's bar back to front.
ladder: Find the pair on the rail first. What is it worth?
Find the two pairs on the rail.
Build it place by place. Which pair on the card makes the tens?
Is that pair one of the six on the card?
Find the letter that takes away. What does it take from?

rules: V, L and D are never repeated
a letter repeats three times at most
V, L and D are never taken away
I from V or X, X from L or C, C from D or M only
a numeral runs from the biggest letter down

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The card redraws row by row and the asked rows light with their values; the asked tile lands on the rail, or the right letters are named under the bays.
Phase 2: Each rail tile writes its amount with an adding bar, then the total climbs to the answer; a build splits by place and the right numeral is laid under the rail.

Phase 3: Each rail tile writes its amount, then the total climbs place by place to the answer; the letters never repeated rise in the tray, take their bars on the card and the strip names them; a build splits by place and the right numeral is laid under the rail.

Phase 4: Each rail tile writes its amount, a taking-away tile with its bar back to front and its pair ringed amber, then the total climbs to the answer; a build lays the right numeral under the rail, its pair ringed amber and the taking-away tile's bar back to front.

voice.opening: Seven letters in the tray. Lift one and read what it is worth.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs
voice.onFinish: You built numerals, and you found what the rules will not let you build.
voice.rules: Spoken on opening, as each phase begins, on each question, on a miss and on the summary page. Every line is printed in the bubble, numbers as words, by the device's own voice (Indian English first). Muting keeps the child's place; unmuting speaks on from the word it reached. If the browser refuses speech until a tap, the first line waits behind a Tap to start cover.

guide.playsOn: none: an Udgam tool opens straight on its phase; the phase's teach lines are spoken first, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

question.en: Lift the V and read it. What is V worth?

items.planQuestion: Which letters stand for fifty and for five hundred?

question.en: Which letters stand for fifty and for five hundred? Put each tile in its place.

items.planAnswer: L is fifty and D is five hundred

items.planQuestion: What are the values of C and of M?

question.en: What are the values of C and of M?

items.planAnswer: C is one hundred and M is one thousand

question.en: Write 36 as a Roman numeral. Build it on the rail, then press enter.

items.planQuestion: What number is XXXIII, and why can thirty-four not be written with four Xs?
items.planAnswer: Thirty-three, and a letter may be repeated at most three times

items.planQuestion: Which three letters may never be repeated?

question.en: Which three letters may never be repeated? Drop two of a letter on the rail to test it.

items.planQuestion: A money box holds 1125 rupees and 250 rupees are spent. Write the balance as a Roman numeral.

question.en: A money box holds ₹1,125 and ₹250 is spent. Write the balance as a Roman numeral.

items.planQuestion: What number is XCVIII, and why is IL not a numeral?
items.planAnswer: Ninety-eight, and I may be subtracted only from V or X

question.en: Write 198 as a Roman numeral. Build it on the rail.

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page; finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

onProgress.done: questions right so far in this phase

hostContract.emits: every event is dispatched on window and, when framed, posted to window.parent as { type: 'event', name, detail }
